notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Biological classification is the systematic arrangement of living organisms into groups based on similarities, differences and evolutionary relationships.
  • Classification makes identification and study of enormous biological diversity easier.
  • Taxonomy deals with identification, nomenclature and classification.
  • Systematics includes taxonomy along with evolutionary relationships among organisms.
  • The basic unit of biological classification is the species.
  • Modern classification increasingly uses molecular, genetic and evolutionary evidence.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Classification → Grouping Organisms

Taxonomy → Identification + Nomenclature + Classification

2. Taxonomy
  • The word taxonomy is derived from Greek taxis meaning arrangement and nomos meaning law.
  • Taxonomy includes identification, naming and classification of organisms.
  • Carl Linnaeus is traditionally called the Father of Taxonomy.
  • Taxonomic groups are called taxa.
  • Singular → Taxon.
  • Plural → Taxa.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Carl Linnaeus → Father of Taxonomy

3. Systematics
  • Systematics studies the diversity of organisms and their evolutionary relationships.
  • It includes classification and phylogeny.
  • Modern systematics uses morphology, anatomy, embryology, biochemistry and DNA evidence.
4. Identification
  • Identification is determining the correct identity of an organism.
  • Identification keys help distinguish organisms using contrasting characteristics.
  • Dichotomous keys generally provide two alternatives at each step.
5. Nomenclature
  • Nomenclature is the scientific naming of organisms.
  • Scientific names provide a universal naming system.
  • Scientific names avoid confusion caused by different local names.
6. Binomial Nomenclature
  • Binomial nomenclature assigns every species a two-part scientific name.
  • First part → Genus.
  • Second part → Specific epithet.
  • Carl Linnaeus formalised widespread use of binomial nomenclature.
📌 Example

Homo sapiens

Homo → Genus

sapiens → Specific epithet

7. Rules of Scientific Names
  • Genus name begins with a capital letter.
  • Specific epithet begins with a lowercase letter.
  • Printed scientific names are italicised.
  • When handwritten, the two words are traditionally underlined separately.
  • Names are generally Latin or Latinised.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Homo sapiens → Correct.

homo Sapiens → Incorrect.

8. Taxonomic Hierarchy

Traditional hierarchy:

  • Kingdom.
  • Phylum or Division.
  • Class.
  • Order.
  • Family.
  • Genus.
  • Species.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species

9. Species
  • Species is the basic unit of classification.
  • Under the biological species concept, members of the same species can interbreed naturally and produce fertile offspring.
  • This concept does not apply perfectly to asexual organisms and fossils.
  • Similar-looking organisms are not necessarily the same species.
10. Genus
  • A genus contains one or more closely related species.
  • Panthera includes lion, tiger, leopard and jaguar.
  • Panthera leo → Lion.
  • Panthera tigris → Tiger.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Panthera → Lion/Tiger Group

11. Family
  • A family contains related genera.
  • Felidae is the cat family.
  • Panthera and Felis belong to Felidae.
12. Order
  • An order contains related families.
  • Carnivora includes families such as Felidae and Canidae.
  • Humans belong to order Primates.
13. Class
  • A class contains related orders.
  • Mammalia is the class containing mammals.
  • Aves is the class containing birds in traditional classification.
14. Phylum
  • A phylum contains related classes.
  • Chordata is the phylum containing vertebrates and related chordates.
  • In botany, the term division has traditionally been used instead of phylum.
15. Kingdom
  • Kingdom is a high traditional taxonomic category.
  • Whittaker's system recognised five kingdoms.
  • Modern domain classification places kingdoms below domains.
16. Early Classification — Aristotle
  • Aristotle classified animals using observable characteristics.
  • He distinguished animals with blood and without blood in an early classification.
  • Aristotle is traditionally called the Father of Zoology.
  • Early systems relied mainly on visible morphology.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Aristotle → Early Animal Classification

17. Theophrastus
  • Theophrastus classified plants based on growth form.
  • He grouped them broadly into herbs, shrubs and trees.
  • He is called the Father of Botany.
18. Two-Kingdom Classification
  • Linnaeus used a two-kingdom system.
  • Kingdom Plantae → Plants.
  • Kingdom Animalia → Animals.
  • Microorganisms did not fit neatly into this system.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Linnaeus → Two Kingdoms → Plantae + Animalia

19. Three-Kingdom Classification
  • Ernst Haeckel proposed a third kingdom called Protista.
  • His three kingdoms were Plantae, Animalia and Protista.
  • Protista accommodated many microscopic organisms.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Haeckel → Protista → Three Kingdoms

20. Four-Kingdom Classification
  • Herbert Copeland proposed a four-kingdom classification.
  • He separated prokaryotes into kingdom Monera.
  • Major groups were Monera, Protista, Plantae and Animalia.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Copeland → Four Kingdoms

21. Five-Kingdom Classification

R. H. Whittaker proposed five kingdoms in 1969:

  • Monera.
  • Protista.
  • Fungi.
  • Plantae.
  • Animalia.
📌 Must-Memorise

Whittaker → Five Kingdom Classification → 1969

22. Basis of Whittaker Classification

Whittaker considered:

  • Cell structure.
  • Body organisation.
  • Mode of nutrition.
  • Reproduction.
  • Phylogenetic relationships.
23. Three-Domain System

Carl Woese and colleagues developed the three-domain concept.

The three domains are:

  • Bacteria.
  • Archaea.
  • Eukarya.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Three Domains → Bacteria + Archaea + Eukarya

24. Carl Woese
  • Carl Woese used ribosomal RNA comparisons.
  • He showed that archaea are fundamentally different from bacteria.
  • The three-domain system became influential around 1990.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Carl Woese → rRNA → Three Domains

25. Domain Bacteria
  • Bacteria are prokaryotic.
  • Their cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus.
  • Most bacterial cell walls contain peptidoglycan.
  • They possess 70S ribosomes.
  • They reproduce mainly by binary fission.
26. Domain Archaea
  • Archaea are prokaryotic.
  • Their cell walls lack typical bacterial peptidoglycan.
  • Their membrane lipids differ chemically from bacterial membrane lipids.
  • Molecular machinery in archaea shows several similarities to eukaryotes.
  • Many archaea live in extreme environments, but many also live in ordinary environments.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Archaea are prokaryotes, but they are not bacteria in the modern three-domain system.

27. Domain Eukarya

Domain Eukarya includes eukaryotic organisms such as:

  • Protists.
  • Fungi.
  • Plants.
  • Animals.
  • Their cells contain membrane-bound nuclei.
28. Kingdom Monera — Traditional Classification
  • Monera contains prokaryotic organisms in Whittaker's system.
  • It includes bacteria and cyanobacteria.
  • Cells lack true nuclei.
  • Membrane-bound organelles are absent.
  • Reproduction is mainly asexual.
📌 TNPSC Note

Monera is important for textbook and exam classification, although modern taxonomy separates Bacteria and Archaea into different domains.

29. Bacteria — Basic Features
  • Bacteria are unicellular prokaryotes.
  • Bacterial DNA is generally located in a nucleoid.
  • Many possess circular chromosomes.
  • Small extra DNA molecules called plasmids may be present.
  • Bacteria usually possess 70S ribosomes.
30. Bacterial Shapes

Major bacterial shapes include:

  • Coccus → Spherical.
  • Bacillus → Rod-shaped.
  • Vibrio → Comma-shaped.
  • Spirillum → Spiral-shaped.
📌 Must-Memorise

Coccus → Sphere

Bacillus → Rod

Vibrio → Comma

Spirillum → Spiral

31. Cocci Arrangements
  • Diplococci → Pairs.
  • Streptococci → Chains.
  • Staphylococci → Grape-like clusters.
  • Arrangement depends on the direction of cell division and attachment.
32. Bacterial Cell Wall
  • Most bacterial cell walls contain peptidoglycan.
  • Peptidoglycan is also called murein.
  • Mycoplasma is a major exception because it lacks a cell wall.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bacterial Wall → Peptidoglycan

Exception → Mycoplasma

33. Mycoplasma
  • Mycoplasma are very small bacteria.
  • They lack a cell wall.
  • Their plasma membrane contains sterols.
  • Their lack of a cell wall makes them naturally resistant to antibiotics that specifically target bacterial cell-wall synthesis.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mycoplasma → No Cell Wall

34. Gram Staining
  • Gram staining divides many bacteria into Gram-positive and Gram-negative groups.
  • The technique was developed by Hans Christian Gram.
  • Gram-positive bacteria retain crystal violet stain and appear purple.
  • Gram-negative bacteria appear pink/red after counterstaining.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hans Christian Gram → Gram Stain

35. Gram-Positive Bacteria
  • Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer.
  • They retain the primary crystal violet-iodine complex.
  • They appear purple after Gram staining.
36. Gram-Negative Bacteria
  • Gram-negative bacteria have a thinner peptidoglycan layer.
  • They possess an outer membrane.
  • They do not retain crystal violet after decolourisation.
  • They appear pink/red after counterstaining.
37. Useful Bacteria

Important beneficial roles include:

  • Nitrogen fixation.
  • Decomposition.
  • Curd formation.
  • Antibiotic production.
  • Sewage treatment.
  • Biotechnology.
38. Lactobacillus
  • Lactobacillus bacteria convert lactose into lactic acid.
  • They contribute to curd and fermented-food production.
  • Lactic acid causes milk proteins to coagulate.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Curd Formation → Lactobacillus

39. Rhizobium
  • Rhizobium forms root nodules in legumes.
  • It fixes atmospheric nitrogen.
  • It is a symbiotic bacterium.
  • It improves soil nitrogen status.
40. Cyanobacteria
  • Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic prokaryotes.
  • They were historically called blue-green algae.
  • They contain chlorophyll a.
  • Some species fix atmospheric nitrogen.

Examples:

  • Nostoc.
  • Anabaena.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Blue-green algae → Actually cyanobacteria → Prokaryotes.

41. Archaea — Major Traditional Types

Common textbook groups include:

  • Methanogens.
  • Halophiles.
  • Thermoacidophiles.
42. Methanogens
  • Methanogens produce methane.
  • They live in anaerobic environments.
  • They occur in marshes and digestive tracts of some animals.
  • They contribute to biogas formation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Methanogens → Methane

43. Halophiles
  • Halophiles thrive in high-salt environments.
  • Many halophilic archaea occur in salt lakes and salt pans.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Halophile → Salt-Loving

44. Thermoacidophiles
  • Thermoacidophiles tolerate high temperature and acidic conditions.
  • Some live in hot acidic springs.
  • They are archaea in traditional textbook examples.
45. Kingdom Protista
  • Protista includes mostly unicellular eukaryotes in Whittaker's system.
  • Some are autotrophic.
  • Some are heterotrophic.
  • Some show characteristics resembling plants, animals or fungi.
  • Protists possess membrane-bound organelles.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Protista → Mostly Unicellular Eukaryotes

46. Amoeba
  • Amoeba is a unicellular eukaryote.
  • It moves using pseudopodia.
  • It captures food by phagocytosis.
  • It reproduces mainly by binary fission.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Amoeba → Pseudopodia

47. Paramecium
  • Paramecium is a unicellular ciliate protist.
  • It moves using cilia.
  • It has an oral groove for feeding.
  • It possesses contractile vacuoles for osmoregulation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Paramecium → Cilia

48. Euglena
  • Euglena has both plant-like and animal-like characteristics.
  • It possesses chloroplasts.
  • It can photosynthesise.
  • It can also use heterotrophic nutrition under suitable conditions.
  • It moves using a flagellum.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Euglena → Mixotrophic Protist

49. Diatoms
  • Diatoms are microscopic photosynthetic protists.
  • Their cell walls form silica-rich shells called frustules.
  • Deposits of diatom shells form diatomaceous earth.
  • Diatoms are important aquatic primary producers.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Diatoms → Silica Cell Wall

50. Dinoflagellates
  • Dinoflagellates are mostly aquatic protists.
  • Many possess two flagella.
  • Some are photosynthetic.
  • Certain species can cause harmful algal blooms and red tides.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dinoflagellates → Red Tide Link

51. Slime Moulds
  • Slime moulds are fungus-like protists in traditional classification.
  • They feed on decaying organic matter.
  • They can form spore-producing structures.
52. Protozoa — Traditional Groups

Traditional protozoan groupings include:

  • Amoeboids.
  • Flagellates.
  • Ciliates.
  • Sporozoans.
  • Modern taxonomy has replaced many of these broad groupings with evolutionary classifications.
53. Plasmodium
  • Plasmodium is a parasitic protist.
  • It causes malaria.
  • It is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes.
  • It belongs to apicomplexan parasites.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Malaria → Plasmodium → Female Anopheles

54. Kingdom Fungi
  • Fungi are eukaryotic.
  • They are heterotrophic.
  • Their cell walls contain chitin.
  • They absorb nutrients after extracellular digestion.
  • Most fungi reproduce through spores.
  • Fungi lack chlorophyll.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fungi → Eukaryotic + Chitin Wall + Heterotrophic

55. Fungal Nutrition

Major nutritional modes include:

  • Saprotrophic.
  • Parasitic.
  • Symbiotic.
  • Fungi secrete enzymes outside their bodies and absorb soluble nutrients.
56. Hypha
  • A hypha is a thread-like fungal filament.
  • A mass of hyphae forms a mycelium.
  • Hyphae may be septate or coenocytic.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hyphae → Mycelium

57. Yeast
  • Yeast is a unicellular fungus.
  • Saccharomyces cerevisiae is used in baking and fermentation.
  • Yeast reproduces commonly by budding.
  • It converts sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide under anaerobic conditions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Yeast → Budding + Fermentation

58. Rhizopus
  • Rhizopus is commonly called bread mould.
  • It is a filamentous fungus.
  • It forms sporangia containing spores.
  • Rhizopus belongs traditionally to lower fungal groups.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bread Mould → Rhizopus

59. Penicillium
  • Penicillium is a fungus.
  • Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin from a Penicillium mould.
  • Some Penicillium species are used in cheese production.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Penicillium → Penicillin

60. Aspergillus
  • Aspergillus includes many mould species.
  • Some species are useful industrially.
  • Some cause disease.
  • Certain Aspergillus species produce aflatoxins.
61. Fungal Classification — Traditional

Traditional school groups include:

  • Phycomycetes.
  • Ascomycetes.
  • Basidiomycetes.
  • Deuteromycetes.
📌 TNPSC Note

Modern fungal taxonomy is molecular and differs from these older textbook groups, but traditional terms remain exam-relevant.

62. Ascomycetes
  • Ascomycetes are called sac fungi.
  • Sexual spores called ascospores are formed inside asci.
  • Yeast and Penicillium are traditionally included.
  • Morels and truffles are also ascomycetes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ascomycetes → Sac Fungi

63. Basidiomycetes
  • Basidiomycetes include mushrooms, puffballs and rusts.
  • Sexual spores called basidiospores are produced on basidia.
  • Many familiar mushrooms belong to this group.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Basidiomycetes → Mushrooms

64. Deuteromycetes
  • Deuteromycetes were historically called imperfect fungi.
  • Sexual stages were unknown when they were classified.
  • Modern molecular classification redistributes these fungi into other groups.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Deuteromycetes → Fungi Imperfecti

65. Lichen
  • Lichen is a symbiotic association between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner.
  • The photosynthetic partner may be an alga or cyanobacterium.
  • The fungus provides protection and absorbs water/minerals.
  • The photosynthetic partner provides organic food.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lichen → Fungus + Alga/Cyanobacterium

66. Lichen as Pollution Indicator
  • Many lichens are sensitive to air pollution.
  • Their abundance can indicate air quality.
  • Sulfur dioxide pollution can reduce sensitive lichen populations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lichen → Air-Pollution Indicator

67. Kingdom Plantae
  • Plants are multicellular eukaryotes.
  • Most are autotrophic and photosynthetic.
  • Plant cell walls contain cellulose.
  • Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll.
  • Plants generally store carbohydrates as starch.
📌 Must-Memorise

Plant Wall → Cellulose

Plant Storage → Starch

68. Traditional Plant Classification

Major traditional groups include:

  • Algae/Thallophyta.
  • Bryophyta.
  • Pteridophyta.
  • Gymnosperms.
  • Angiosperms.
69. Cryptogams
  • Cryptogams are plants or plant-like organisms with inconspicuous reproductive structures and no seeds.
  • Traditional cryptogams include algae, bryophytes and pteridophytes.
  • They reproduce through spores rather than seeds.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cryptogams → Seedless

70. Phanerogams
  • Phanerogams are seed-producing plants.
  • They include gymnosperms and angiosperms.
  • Their reproductive structures are more conspicuous.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Phanerogams → Seed Plants

71. Algae
  • Algae are mostly aquatic photosynthetic organisms.
  • Their body is often a simple thallus.
  • They lack true roots, stems and leaves in traditional descriptions.
  • Algae range from unicellular forms to large multicellular seaweeds.
72. Green Algae
  • Green algae are traditionally grouped as Chlorophyceae.
  • Chlorophyll a and b are prominent pigments.
  • Starch is the major stored food.
  • Examples include Chlamydomonas, Spirogyra and Ulva.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Green Algae → Chlorophyll a+b → Starch

73. Brown Algae
  • Brown algae are traditionally grouped as Phaeophyceae.
  • Fucoxanthin gives the characteristic brown colour.
  • They are mainly marine.
  • Laminaria and Sargassum are examples.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Brown Algae → Fucoxanthin

74. Red Algae
  • Red algae belong traditionally to Rhodophyceae.
  • Phycoerythrin is an important red pigment.
  • Many are marine.
  • Gelidium and Gracilaria are examples.
  • Agar is obtained from certain red algae.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Red Algae → Phycoerythrin → Agar

75. Bryophytes
  • Bryophytes are small non-vascular land plants.
  • They lack true vascular tissue.
  • They require water for sexual reproduction.
  • They are called amphibians of the plant kingdom.
  • Gametophyte is the dominant generation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bryophytes → Amphibians of Plant Kingdom

76. Bryophyte Examples

Examples include:

  • Riccia.
  • Marchantia.
  • Funaria.
  • Sphagnum.
  • Mosses and liverworts are bryophytes.
77. Sphagnum
  • Sphagnum is a peat moss.
  • It can hold large amounts of water.
  • Accumulated partially decomposed Sphagnum contributes to peat formation.
78. Pteridophytes
  • Pteridophytes are vascular seedless plants.
  • They possess true roots, stems and leaves.
  • They reproduce by spores.
  • They are called vascular cryptogams.
  • Sporophyte is the dominant generation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pteridophytes → First Vascular Land Plants in Traditional Sequence

79. Pteridophyte Examples
  • Ferns.
  • Selaginella.
  • Equisetum.
  • Lycopodium.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fern → Pteridophyte

80. Gymnosperms
  • Gymnosperms are seed-producing vascular plants.
  • Their seeds are not enclosed within fruits.
  • They are called naked-seeded plants.
  • They generally bear reproductive cones.
  • They do not produce true fruits.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gymnosperm → Naked Seeds

81. Gymnosperm Examples
  • Cycas.
  • Pinus.
  • Cedrus.
  • Gnetum.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cycas + Pinus → Gymnosperms

82. Cycas
  • Cycas resembles a palm but is a gymnosperm.
  • It is dioecious, with male and female reproductive structures on separate plants.
  • Coralloid roots may contain nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.
83. Angiosperms
  • Angiosperms are flowering plants.
  • Their seeds develop inside ovaries.
  • The ovary develops into a fruit after fertilisation.
  • Angiosperms are the largest group of land plants.
  • They show double fertilisation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Angiosperm → Flower + Enclosed Seed + Fruit

84. Double Fertilisation
  • Double fertilisation is characteristic of angiosperms.
  • One male gamete fuses with egg to form zygote.
  • Another male gamete fuses with polar nuclei/central cell to form primary endosperm nucleus.
  • This produces embryo and endosperm.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Double Fertilisation → Angiosperms

85. Monocotyledons

Traditional monocot features include:

  • One cotyledon.
  • Parallel leaf venation.
  • Fibrous root system.
  • Floral parts commonly in multiples of three.
  • Vascular bundles usually scattered in stems.
📌 Examples

Rice, wheat, maize, banana, coconut.

86. Dicotyledons

Traditional dicot features include:

  • Two cotyledons.
  • Reticulate/net leaf venation.
  • Taproot system commonly present.
  • Floral parts commonly in multiples of four or five.
  • Stem vascular bundles commonly arranged in a ring.
📌 Examples

Bean, pea, mango, sunflower.

87. Monocot vs Dicot — Must Memorise

Monocot:

  • 1 cotyledon.
  • Parallel venation.
  • Fibrous roots.
  • Floral parts ×3.

Dicot:

  • 2 cotyledons.
  • Reticulate venation.
  • Taproot.
  • Floral parts ×4 or ×5.
88. Kingdom Animalia
  • Animals are multicellular eukaryotes.
  • They are heterotrophic.
  • Their cells lack cell walls.
  • Most animals can move actively during at least one life stage.
  • Animals generally reproduce sexually, though asexual reproduction also occurs in some.
89. Basis of Animal Classification

Important criteria include:

  • Level of organisation.
  • Body symmetry.
  • Number of germ layers.
  • Body cavity.
  • Segmentation.
  • Presence or absence of notochord.
90. Body Symmetry

Major types include:

  • Asymmetry.
  • Radial symmetry.
  • Bilateral symmetry.
91. Asymmetry
  • An asymmetrical animal cannot be divided into equal mirror halves through any plane.
  • Many sponges are asymmetrical.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Porifera → Often Asymmetrical

92. Radial Symmetry
  • Body parts are arranged around a central axis.
  • Multiple planes can produce similar halves.
  • Adult cnidarians show radial symmetry.
  • Adult echinoderms show secondary radial symmetry.
93. Bilateral Symmetry
  • Only one principal plane divides the body into right and left mirror halves.
  • Most higher animals show bilateral symmetry.
  • Bilateral symmetry is associated with cephalisation.
94. Germ Layers

Embryonic germ layers are:

  • Ectoderm.
  • Mesoderm.
  • Endoderm.
95. Diploblastic Animals
  • Diploblastic animals develop mainly from two germ layers.
  • Ectoderm and endoderm are present.
  • Cnidarians are diploblastic.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cnidaria → Diploblastic

96. Triploblastic Animals
  • Triploblastic animals develop from three germ layers.
  • Ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm are present.
  • Most bilaterally symmetrical animals are triploblastic.
97. Body Cavity

Major categories include:

  • Acoelomate.
  • Pseudocoelomate.
  • Coelomate.
98. Acoelomate
  • Acoelomates lack a body cavity between gut and body wall.
  • Platyhelminthes are acoelomates.
99. Pseudocoelomate
  • Pseudocoelomates have a body cavity not completely lined by mesoderm.
  • Nematodes are classic pseudocoelomates.
100. True Coelom
  • True coelom is completely lined by mesoderm.
  • Annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms and chordates are coelomate in standard classification.
101. Porifera
  • Porifera means pore-bearing animals.
  • They are commonly called sponges.
  • They are mostly marine.
  • Their bodies contain numerous pores.
  • A canal system circulates water.
  • Cellular level of organisation is present.
  • Choanocytes or collar cells are characteristic.
📌 Examples

Sycon, Spongilla, Euspongia.

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Porifera → Pores + Canal System

102. Spongilla
  • Spongilla is a freshwater sponge.
  • Most other commonly cited sponges are marine.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Porifera are mostly marine, but Spongilla is freshwater.

103. Cnidaria / Coelenterata
  • Cnidarians are aquatic, mostly marine animals.
  • They show radial symmetry.
  • They are diploblastic.
  • They possess specialised stinging cells called cnidocytes.
  • Nematocysts occur inside cnidocytes.
  • Gastrovascular cavity has a single opening.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cnidaria → Cnidocytes/Stinging Cells

104. Cnidarian Examples
  • Hydra.
  • Obelia.
  • Jellyfish.
  • Sea anemone.
  • Corals.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hydra → Cnidarian

105. Coral Reefs
  • Corals are cnidarians.
  • Many reef-building corals secrete calcium-carbonate skeletons.
  • They often live symbiotically with photosynthetic dinoflagellates.
  • Coral reefs support high biodiversity.
106. Platyhelminthes
  • Platyhelminthes are flatworms.
  • They are bilaterally symmetrical.
  • They are triploblastic.
  • They are acoelomate.
  • Many are parasitic.
📌 Examples

Planaria, Taenia, Fasciola.

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Platyhelminthes → Flatworms

107. Taenia
  • Taenia is a tapeworm.
  • It is an intestinal parasite.
  • It lacks a complete digestive tract.
  • Nutrients are absorbed through the body surface.
108. Nematoda
  • Nematodes are roundworms.
  • They are unsegmented.
  • They are bilaterally symmetrical.
  • They are pseudocoelomate.
  • Many are parasites, though many are free-living.
📌 Examples

Ascaris, Wuchereria, hookworm.

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nematoda → Roundworms

109. Ascaris
  • Ascaris is an intestinal roundworm parasite.
  • It causes ascariasis.
  • Male and female worms are separate.
110. Wuchereria
  • Wuchereria is a parasitic nematode.
  • It causes lymphatic filariasis.
  • It is transmitted by mosquitoes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Filariasis → Wuchereria

111. Annelida
  • Annelids are segmented worms.
  • They possess a true coelom.
  • They show metameric segmentation.
  • They have a closed circulatory system.
📌 Examples

Earthworm, leech, Nereis.

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Annelida → Segmented Worms

112. Earthworm
  • Earthworms are annelids.
  • They improve soil aeration and mixing.
  • Their excreta contribute to soil fertility.
  • Earthworms are used in vermicomposting.
113. Arthropoda
  • Arthropoda is the largest animal phylum.
  • Arthropods have jointed appendages.
  • Their bodies have an exoskeleton made mainly of chitin.
  • They possess an open circulatory system.
  • Their body is segmented.
📌 Must-Memorise

Largest Animal Phylum → Arthropoda

114. Arthropod Groups

Major groups include:

  • Insects.
  • Arachnids.
  • Crustaceans.
  • Myriapods.
115. Insects
  • Insects have three body regions: head, thorax and abdomen.
  • They possess three pairs of legs.
  • Usually one pair of antennae.
  • Many have one or two pairs of wings.
  • Respiration commonly occurs through tracheae.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Insect → 6 Legs

116. Arachnids
  • Arachnids have four pairs of walking legs.
  • They lack antennae.
  • Spiders, scorpions, ticks and mites are arachnids.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Arachnid → 8 Legs

117. Crustaceans
  • Crustaceans are mainly aquatic arthropods.
  • They generally possess two pairs of antennae.
  • Examples include prawns, crabs and lobsters.
  • Respiration commonly occurs through gills.
118. Mollusca
  • Molluscs have soft unsegmented bodies.
  • Many possess a shell.
  • A muscular foot is commonly present.
  • Mantle secretes the shell in many species.
  • Radula is present in many molluscs but absent in bivalves.
📌 Examples

Snail, oyster, mussel, octopus, squid.

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mollusca → Soft Body + Muscular Foot

119. Octopus
  • Octopus is a mollusc.
  • It belongs to class Cephalopoda.
  • Its foot is modified into arms around the head.
  • It has a highly developed nervous system.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Octopus → Mollusc, not fish.

120. Echinodermata
  • Echinoderms are exclusively marine.
  • Adults show pentaradial symmetry.
  • Larvae are bilaterally symmetrical.
  • They possess a water vascular system.
  • Their internal skeleton contains calcareous plates.
📌 Examples

Starfish, sea urchin, sea cucumber.

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Echinodermata → Water Vascular System

121. Starfish
  • Starfish is an echinoderm.
  • It is not a true fish.
  • Tube feet are part of its water vascular system.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Starfish → Echinoderm, not fish.

122. Hemichordata
  • Hemichordates are marine worm-like animals.
  • Body is divided into proboscis, collar and trunk.
  • Balanoglossus is a common example.
  • They possess pharyngeal gill slits.
123. Chordata

All chordates possess at least during some stage:

  • Notochord.
  • Dorsal hollow nerve cord.
  • Pharyngeal gill slits.
  • Post-anal tail.
  • Endostyle or thyroid-related structure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chordate → Notochord + Dorsal Hollow Nerve Cord

124. Notochord
  • Notochord is a flexible supporting rod.
  • It lies along the dorsal side of the body.
  • In vertebrates, it is largely replaced by the vertebral column during development.
125. Vertebrates
  • Vertebrates are chordates with a vertebral column.
  • They possess an internal skeleton.
  • Major traditional groups include fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
126. Pisces — Traditional Fish Group
  • Fishes are aquatic vertebrates.
  • They breathe mainly through gills.
  • Fins are used for locomotion.
  • Most have a two-chambered heart.
  • They are ectothermic.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fish Heart → 2 Chambers

127. Cartilaginous Fishes
  • Chondrichthyes are cartilaginous fishes.
  • Their skeleton is made mainly of cartilage.
  • Examples include sharks and rays.
  • Gill slits are usually not covered by an operculum.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Shark → Cartilaginous Fish

128. Bony Fishes
  • Osteichthyes possess a bony skeleton.
  • Gills are usually covered by an operculum.
  • Swim bladder is present in many bony fishes.
  • Examples include rohu and catla.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rohu + Catla → Bony Fishes

129. Amphibia
  • Amphibians live partly in water and partly on land.
  • Their skin is generally moist and lacks scales.
  • Larvae commonly breathe through gills.
  • Adults use lungs and skin.
  • Most have a three-chambered heart.
  • They are ectothermic.
📌 Examples

Frog, toad, salamander.

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Amphibian Heart → 3 Chambers

130. Frog
  • Frog undergoes metamorphosis.
  • Tadpole is the aquatic larval stage.
  • Adult frog breathes through lungs and moist skin.
  • Fertilisation is usually external in many frogs.
131. Reptilia
  • Reptiles have dry, keratinised scales.
  • They breathe with lungs.
  • Fertilisation is internal.
  • Most reptiles lay shelled amniotic eggs.
  • They are ectothermic.
  • Most have a three-chambered heart.
📌 Examples

Snake, lizard, turtle, crocodile.

132. Crocodile Exception
  • Crocodiles have a four-chambered heart.
  • This differs from most reptiles, which have incompletely divided three-chambered hearts.
📌 Must-Memorise

Crocodile → 4-Chambered Heart

133. Aves
  • Birds belong traditionally to class Aves.
  • Their bodies are covered with feathers.
  • Forelimbs are modified into wings.
  • They are endothermic.
  • They possess a four-chambered heart.
  • Birds lay hard-shelled eggs.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bird → Feathers + 4-Chambered Heart

134. Bird Bones
  • Many bird bones are lightweight and contain air spaces.
  • Such bones are called pneumatic bones.
  • This reduces body mass for flight, though not all bird bones are hollow.
135. Mammalia
  • Mammals possess mammary glands.
  • Their bodies usually have hair.
  • They are endothermic.
  • They possess a four-chambered heart.
  • A muscular diaphragm separates thoracic and abdominal cavities.
  • Most mammals give birth to live young.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mammals → Mammary Glands + Hair + Diaphragm

136. Monotremes
  • Monotremes are egg-laying mammals.
  • Platypus is a monotreme.
  • Echidna is another monotreme.
  • They still possess mammary glands.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Not all mammals give birth to live young.

137. Marsupials
  • Marsupials give birth to relatively underdeveloped young.
  • Further development often occurs in a pouch.
  • Kangaroo is a classic marsupial.
  • Koala is another marsupial.
138. Placental Mammals
  • Placental mammals develop embryos connected to the mother through a placenta.
  • Humans, dogs, elephants and whales are placental mammals.
  • They form the majority of living mammal species.
139. Aquatic Mammals
  • Whale and dolphin are mammals.
  • They breathe air using lungs.
  • They give birth to live young.
  • They feed their young with milk.
  • They must surface to breathe.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Whale and dolphin → Mammals, not fishes.

140. Bat
  • Bat is a mammal.
  • Bats are the only mammals capable of sustained powered flight.
  • Many bats use echolocation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Flying Mammal → Bat

141. Vertebrate Heart Chambers
  • Fish → 2 chambers.
  • Amphibians → 3 chambers.
  • Most reptiles → 3 chambers.
  • Crocodile → 4 chambers.
  • Birds → 4 chambers.
  • Mammals → 4 chambers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fish 2

Frog 3

Crocodile/Bird/Mammal 4

142. Ectotherms
  • Ectotherms depend largely on external environmental heat sources to regulate body temperature.
  • Fishes, amphibians and reptiles are generally ectothermic.
  • The old term cold-blooded is less precise.
143. Endotherms
  • Birds and mammals generate substantial body heat metabolically.
  • They maintain relatively stable internal temperatures.
  • They are called endothermic.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Birds + Mammals → Endothermic

144. Invertebrates
  • Invertebrates lack a vertebral column.
  • They include most animal species.
  • Major invertebrate phyla include Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca and Echinodermata.
145. Vertebrates vs Invertebrates
  • Vertebrates possess a vertebral column.
  • Invertebrates lack a vertebral column.
  • Both belong to kingdom Animalia.
  • Vertebrates represent only a small fraction of total animal diversity.
146. Virus
  • Viruses are acellular infectious agents.
  • They are not placed comfortably within the traditional five kingdoms.
  • They contain either DNA or RNA as genetic material.
  • A protein coat called capsid surrounds the genome.
  • Some viruses possess an outer lipid envelope.
  • Viruses reproduce only inside living host cells.
📌 Must-Memorise

Virus → Acellular + Obligate Intracellular Parasite

147. Capsid
  • Capsid is the protein coat of a virus.
  • It is composed of protein subunits called capsomeres.
  • Capsid protects viral genetic material.
148. Bacteriophage
  • A bacteriophage is a virus that infects bacteria.
  • Many bacteriophages have a head-and-tail structure.
  • They are important tools in molecular biology.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bacteriophage → Virus of Bacteria

149. Tobacco Mosaic Virus
  • TMV stands for Tobacco Mosaic Virus.
  • It infects tobacco and related plants.
  • TMV contains RNA as genetic material.
  • It was important in early virus research.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

TMV → RNA Virus of Plants

150. Dmitri Ivanovsky
  • Dmitri Ivanovsky demonstrated that the infectious agent causing tobacco mosaic disease could pass through filters that retained bacteria.
  • His work in 1892 was foundational in virology.
151. Martinus Beijerinck
  • Beijerinck further studied the tobacco mosaic agent.
  • He described it as a contagious living fluid in historical terminology.
  • His work helped establish the concept of viruses.
152. W. M. Stanley
  • Wendell Meredith Stanley crystallised Tobacco Mosaic Virus in 1935.
  • This demonstrated unusual chemical-like properties of viruses.
  • He later shared the 1946 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

W. M. Stanley → Crystallised TMV → 1935

153. Viroid
  • Viroids are very small infectious RNA molecules.
  • They lack a protein coat.
  • They mainly infect plants.
  • The term viroid is associated with Theodor Diener.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Viroid → Naked Infectious RNA

154. Prion
  • Prions are infectious misfolded proteins.
  • They contain no DNA or RNA.
  • They cause certain neurodegenerative diseases.
  • Stanley Prusiner received the 1997 Nobel Prize for prion research.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Prion → Infectious Protein

155. Virus vs Bacterium
  • Virus → Acellular.
  • Bacterium → Cellular prokaryote.
  • Virus → Requires host cell for replication.
  • Bacterium → Can reproduce independently under suitable conditions.
  • Antibiotics do not treat ordinary viral infections.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Antibiotics → Bacteria, not viruses.

156. Important Classification Scientist Pairs
  • Aristotle → Early animal classification.
  • Theophrastus → Plant classification.
  • Linnaeus → Taxonomy and binomial nomenclature.
  • Haeckel → Protista/three-kingdom system.
  • Copeland → Four kingdoms.
  • Whittaker → Five kingdoms.
  • Woese → Three domains.
  • Hans Christian Gram → Gram stain.
157. Important Dates
  • Linnaeus's Species Plantarum → 1753.
  • Haeckel's three-kingdom concept → 19th century.
  • Whittaker's five-kingdom system → 1969.
  • Woese three-domain concept → Late 20th century, formalised around 1990.
  • Ivanovsky virus-filter experiment → 1892.
  • TMV crystallised by Stanley → 1935.
158. Must-Memorise Kingdom Features

Monera:

  • Prokaryotic.
  • Mostly unicellular.
  • No true nucleus.

Protista:

  • Eukaryotic.
  • Mostly unicellular.

Fungi:

  • Eukaryotic.
  • Chitin wall.
  • Heterotrophic absorption.

Plantae:

  • Eukaryotic.
  • Cellulose wall.
  • Mostly photosynthetic.

Animalia:

  • Eukaryotic.
  • No cell wall.
  • Heterotrophic ingestion.
159. Must-Memorise Plant Groups
  • Algae → Simple thalloid forms.
  • Bryophytes → Non-vascular amphibians of plant kingdom.
  • Pteridophytes → Vascular seedless plants.
  • Gymnosperms → Naked seeds.
  • Angiosperms → Enclosed seeds and flowers.
160. Must-Memorise Animal Phyla
  • Porifera → Pores.
  • Cnidaria → Stinging cells.
  • Platyhelminthes → Flatworms.
  • Nematoda → Roundworms.
  • Annelida → Segmented worms.
  • Arthropoda → Jointed appendages.
  • Mollusca → Soft body.
  • Echinodermata → Water vascular system.
  • Chordata → Notochord.
161. TNPSC Traps
  • Species is the basic taxonomic unit.
  • Linnaeus is Father of Taxonomy.
  • Whittaker proposed five kingdoms in 1969.
  • Woese proposed the three-domain framework.
  • Monera is a traditional kingdom, not a modern domain.
  • Archaea are prokaryotic.
  • Archaea are not ordinary bacteria.
  • Bacteria possess 70S ribosomes.
  • Bacterial wall usually contains peptidoglycan.
  • Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall.
  • Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes.
  • Blue-green algae are actually cyanobacteria.
  • Protists are eukaryotic.
  • Amoeba moves with pseudopodia.
  • Paramecium moves with cilia.
  • Euglena moves with flagellum and can be mixotrophic.
  • Diatoms have silica walls.
  • Fungal walls contain chitin.
  • Yeast is a fungus.
  • Yeast commonly reproduces by budding.
  • Rhizopus is bread mould.
  • Lichen is fungus + photosynthetic partner.
  • Bryophytes are called amphibians of the plant kingdom.
  • Pteridophytes are vascular cryptogams.
  • Gymnosperms have naked seeds.
  • Angiosperms show double fertilisation.
  • Monocots have one cotyledon.
  • Dicots traditionally have two cotyledons.
  • Arthropoda is the largest animal phylum.
  • Insects have six legs.
  • Arachnids have eight legs.
  • Octopus is a mollusc.
  • Starfish is an echinoderm.
  • Starfish is not a fish.
  • Whale is a mammal.
  • Dolphin is a mammal.
  • Bat is a mammal.
  • Crocodile has a four-chambered heart.
  • Birds and mammals have four-chambered hearts.
  • Fish generally have two-chambered hearts.
  • Amphibians generally have three-chambered hearts.
  • Viruses are acellular.
  • Viroids are naked infectious RNA.
  • Prions are infectious proteins.
  • Antibiotics do not kill viruses.
162. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Linnaeus → Taxonomy.
  • Species → Basic unit.
  • Whittaker → 5 kingdoms.
  • Woese → 3 domains.
  • Monera → Prokaryote.
  • Protista → Unicellular eukaryote.
  • Fungi → Chitin.
  • Plants → Cellulose.
  • Animals → No wall.
  • Coccus → Sphere.
  • Bacillus → Rod.
  • Vibrio → Comma.
  • Mycoplasma → No wall.
  • Amoeba → Pseudopodia.
  • Paramecium → Cilia.
  • Euglena → Flagellum.
  • Diatom → Silica.
  • Yeast → Budding.
  • Lichen → Fungus + alga.
  • Bryophyte → Amphibian plant.
  • Pteridophyte → Vascular cryptogam.
  • Gymnosperm → Naked seed.
  • Angiosperm → Covered seed.
  • Porifera → Pores.
  • Cnidaria → Stinging cells.
  • Platyhelminthes → Flat.
  • Nematoda → Round.
  • Annelida → Segmented.
  • Arthropoda → Jointed legs.
  • Mollusca → Soft.
  • Echinoderm → Water vascular.
  • Chordata → Notochord.
  • Fish → 2-heart chambers.
  • Frog → 3.
  • Crocodile → 4.
  • Bird → 4.
  • Mammal → 4.
  • Virus → Acellular.
  • Viroid → RNA.
  • Prion → Protein.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • Study of classification, identification and naming? → Taxonomy.
  • Father of Taxonomy? → Carl Linnaeus.
  • Basic unit of classification? → Species.
  • Two-word scientific naming system? → Binomial nomenclature.
  • First word of scientific name? → Genus.
  • Second word? → Specific epithet.
  • Genus written with? → Initial capital letter.
  • Specific epithet written with? → Lowercase initial.
  • Correct human scientific name? → Homo sapiens.
  • Traditional taxonomic hierarchy? → Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.
  • Who proposed two kingdoms? → Linnaeus.
  • Two kingdoms? → Plantae and Animalia.
  • Who introduced Protista as third kingdom? → Ernst Haeckel.
  • Who proposed four kingdoms? → Herbert Copeland.
  • Who proposed five kingdoms? → R. H. Whittaker.
  • Year of Whittaker classification? → 1969.
  • Five kingdoms? → Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
  • Who proposed three-domain system? → Carl Woese.
  • Three domains? → Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya.
  • Basis strongly used by Woese? → Ribosomal RNA.
  • Are bacteria prokaryotic? → Yes.
  • Do bacteria have a membrane-bound nucleus? → No.
  • Bacterial ribosomes? → 70S.
  • Main bacterial wall material? → Peptidoglycan.
  • Bacterium lacking cell wall? → Mycoplasma.
  • Spherical bacteria? → Cocci.
  • Rod-shaped bacteria? → Bacilli.
  • Comma-shaped bacteria? → Vibrios.
  • Spiral bacteria? → Spirilla.
  • Gram stain developed by? → Hans Christian Gram.
  • Gram-positive bacteria appear? → Purple.
  • Gram-negative bacteria appear? → Pink/red.
  • Bacterium associated with curd? → Lactobacillus.
  • Legume nitrogen-fixing bacterium? → Rhizobium.
  • Blue-green algae are actually? → Cyanobacteria.
  • Nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria examples? → Nostoc and Anabaena.
  • Methane-producing archaea? → Methanogens.
  • Salt-loving archaea? → Halophiles.
  • Heat-and-acid-loving archaea? → Thermoacidophiles.
  • Kingdom of mostly unicellular eukaryotes in Whittaker system? → Protista.
  • Amoeba movement? → Pseudopodia.
  • Paramecium movement? → Cilia.
  • Euglena movement? → Flagellum.
  • Euglena nutrition? → Mixotrophic.
  • Diatom wall composed of? → Silica.
  • Red tides commonly linked with? → Certain dinoflagellates.
  • Malaria parasite? → Plasmodium.
  • Vector of malaria? → Female Anopheles mosquito.
  • Fungal cell wall? → Chitin.
  • Fungi possess chlorophyll? → No.
  • Mass of fungal hyphae? → Mycelium.
  • Unicellular fungus? → Yeast.
  • Yeast reproduction commonly? → Budding.
  • Bread mould? → Rhizopus.
  • Fungus associated with penicillin? → Penicillium.
  • Sac fungi? → Ascomycetes.
  • Mushroom group? → Basidiomycetes.
  • Imperfect fungi traditional name? → Deuteromycetes.
  • Lichen association? → Fungus + alga/cyanobacterium.
  • Lichens can indicate? → Air pollution.
  • Plant cell wall? → Cellulose.
  • Plant stored carbohydrate? → Starch.
  • Traditional seedless plant groups? → Algae, bryophytes and pteridophytes.
  • Plants called amphibians of plant kingdom? → Bryophytes.
  • Why bryophytes called amphibians? → Live on land but require water for sexual reproduction.
  • Examples of bryophytes? → Marchantia, Funaria, Riccia, Sphagnum.
  • Vascular cryptogams? → Pteridophytes.
  • Examples of pteridophytes? → Fern, Selaginella, Equisetum.
  • Naked-seeded plants? → Gymnosperms.
  • Gymnosperm examples? → Cycas and Pinus.
  • Flowering plants? → Angiosperms.
  • Unique fertilisation feature of angiosperms? → Double fertilisation.
  • Monocot cotyledons? → One.
  • Dicot cotyledons? → Two.
  • Monocot venation? → Parallel.
  • Dicot venation? → Reticulate.
  • Monocot root system generally? → Fibrous.
  • Dicot root system generally? → Taproot.
  • Basic animal classification criteria? → Symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation and notochord.
  • Animal phylum with pores? → Porifera.
  • Characteristic cells of Porifera? → Choanocytes.
  • Freshwater sponge? → Spongilla.
  • Phylum with cnidocytes? → Cnidaria.
  • Examples of cnidarians? → Hydra, jellyfish, sea anemone and coral.
  • Flatworm phylum? → Platyhelminthes.
  • Tapeworm belongs to? → Platyhelminthes.
  • Roundworm phylum? → Nematoda.
  • Ascaris belongs to? → Nematoda.
  • Filariasis worm? → Wuchereria.
  • Segmented worms? → Annelida.
  • Earthworm phylum? → Annelida.
  • Largest animal phylum? → Arthropoda.
  • Characteristic feature of arthropods? → Jointed appendages and chitinous exoskeleton.
  • Number of legs in insects? → Six.
  • Number of walking legs in arachnids? → Eight.
  • Examples of arachnids? → Spider, scorpion, tick and mite.
  • Prawn and crab belong to? → Crustacea/Arthropoda.
  • Soft-bodied animal phylum? → Mollusca.
  • Snail belongs to? → Mollusca.
  • Octopus belongs to? → Mollusca.
  • Phylum with water vascular system? → Echinodermata.
  • Starfish belongs to? → Echinodermata.
  • Are echinoderms marine? → Yes, exclusively marine.
  • Chordates possess? → Notochord and dorsal hollow nerve cord.
  • Vertebrate means? → Chordate possessing vertebral column.
  • Traditional vertebrate groups? → Fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
  • Fish respiration? → Gills.
  • Fish heart chambers? → Two.
  • Shark skeleton? → Cartilage.
  • Rohu and catla are? → Bony fishes.
  • Amphibian heart? → Usually three chambers.
  • Frog larva? → Tadpole.
  • Reptile skin? → Dry and scaly.
  • Most reptile hearts? → Three chambers.
  • Reptile with four-chambered heart? → Crocodile.
  • Bird heart? → Four chambers.
  • Bird body covering? → Feathers.
  • Light air-filled bird bones called? → Pneumatic bones.
  • Mammalian characteristic glands? → Mammary glands.
  • Mammal respiratory muscle separating chest and abdomen? → Diaphragm.
  • Mammal heart? → Four chambers.
  • Egg-laying mammals? → Monotremes.
  • Examples? → Platypus and echidna.
  • Pouched mammals? → Marsupials.
  • Example? → Kangaroo.
  • Whale is fish or mammal? → Mammal.
  • Dolphin? → Mammal.
  • Flying mammal? → Bat.
  • Birds and mammals are? → Endothermic.
  • Fishes, amphibians and reptiles generally? → Ectothermic.
  • Virus is cellular or acellular? → Acellular.
  • Viral genetic material? → Either DNA or RNA.
  • Protein coat of virus? → Capsid.
  • Virus infecting bacteria? → Bacteriophage.
  • TMV full form? → Tobacco Mosaic Virus.
  • TMV genome? → RNA.
  • Who performed early filterable-virus experiment? → Dmitri Ivanovsky.
  • Who crystallised TMV? → W. M. Stanley.
  • Year TMV crystallised? → 1935.
  • Viroid consists mainly of? → Infectious RNA without protein coat.
  • Prion consists of? → Infectious misfolded protein.
  • Do antibiotics cure ordinary viral infections? → No.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → Whittaker → 5 kingdoms; Woese → 3 domains; Bryophyte → amphibian plant; Gymnosperm → naked seed; Arthropoda → largest animal phylum; Chordata → notochord; Virus → acellular.
